newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish parliament approves health care reform.
newsitem.headline: Polish parliament approves health care reform.

text.p: The lower house of parliament on Wednesday approved a bill reforming Poland's inefficient communist-era health care service as doctors maintained a nationwide strike for more pay and funding for the system.

A bill, adopted in a 233-to-115 vote with 14 abstentions, provides for the creation of special health care funds to which all citizens would contribute 10 percent of their income on a tax-deductible basis.
The funds will cover costs of medical consultations, basic drugs and regular hospital treatment after patients enter agreements with public health care units.
Patients would be allowed to choose their doctors and hospitals and thus funds allocated to a medical care unit would depend of the amount of service it provides.
Health Minister Ryszard Zochowski said the regulations, to become effective in 1999, will introduce elements of the free market to the system, now centralised and directly financed from the budget.
"The reform will improve the situation of the health care service very soon after its implementation. Hospitals and clinics will make efforts to attract patients," Zochowski said.
The budget will continue to provide the means for medical schools and the construction of hospitals. It will also contribute premiums for those with no earnings.
Under the current system, health care should in theory be given free to all Poles paying social security premiums.

But the quality of medical service in state-owned hospitals is often poor and patients face long waits for complicated surgery. Newspapers report cases of bribes given to secure places in better hospitals.

Many private clinics providing high-quality service have sprouted since the fall of communism in 1989, but few can afford them in a country where an average gross months salary is about 1,000 zlotys ($350).

The underpaid doctors went on strike eight days ago, demanding a salary rise to about 3,000 zlotys (more than $1,000) a month and a rise in budget spending on health care to six percent of gross domestic product from four percent.
The strike, organised by a trade union grouping one third of Poland's 90,000 doctors, has affected two-thirds of hospitals and half of out-patient clinics.

The doctors are continuing to treat emergency and life threatening cases and have excluded cancer, psychiatric, children's and maternity wards from the stoppage, but routine examinations and operations are being cancelled.
The reform bill, which still needs to clear the Senate and be signed by President Aleksander Kwasniewski, was criticised by the opposition to the ruling left-wing coalition.

Poland plans to spend 18.2 billion zlotys ($6.5 billion) on health care next year, about eight percent more in real terms than in 1996. This represents some $170 per capita, which is about one fifth the average in industrialised nations.
